extracted.intended_audience: general readers; students and researchers of media law, broadcasting, and comedy history
extracted.subtask_description: Information and standards about which profane words have been treated as broadcast-indecent in the United States (the 'Seven Dirty Words'), the legal and regulatory history around broadcasting those words, and common broadcaster practices for handling expletives.

rubrics_metrics.name: The seven dirty words (Carlin's list)
rubrics_metrics.description: The words, in the order Carlin listed them, are: "shit", "piss", "fuck", "cunt", "cocksucker", "motherfucker", and "tits".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These words were considered highly inappropriate and unsuitable for broadcast on the public airwaves in the United States, and thus were avoided in scripted material and bleep censored in the rare cases in which they were used. Carlin later sometimes expanded or revised the list (e.g., adding "fart", "turd", "twat" in later routines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indecency regulation established in FCC v. Pacifica
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court (1978) ruled that the FCC's declaratory ruling upholding a 1973 complaint about Carlin's routine did not violate the First or Fifth Amendment (limited to the specific broadcast at issue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This decision formally established indecency regulation in American broadcasting and defined the extent to which the federal government could regulate speech on broadcast television and radio; the Court limited the scope to the specific broadcast and did not decide application to other material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safe harbor provision (time-based allowance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court later established the safe harbor provision that grants broadcasters the right to broadcast indecent (but not obscene) material between the hours of 10 pm and 6 am.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The safe harbor is premised on the presumption that few children would be watching during those hours; indecent (non-obscene) content may be aired in that window without the same regulatory risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: No official, specific FCC list of prohibited words
rubrics_metrics.description: The FCC has never maintained a specific list of words prohibited from the airwaves during the time period from 6 am to 10 pm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite the absence of an official list, the seven dirty words have been assumed likely to elicit indecency-related action by the FCC if uttered on TV or radio during protected hours, leading broadcasters to self-censor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual determination of offensiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: As George Carlin observed, there is no consistent standard — 'It's the thrust of the sentence that makes them either good or bad' — and enforcement/standards are inconsistent and context-dependent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: publications' inconsistent redaction styles (e.g., f**k vs f*** vs 'expletive deleted'), and the Court's refusal to decide whether identical words in other contexts (Shakespeare, the Bible) would be treated the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fleeting expletives legal treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: FCC regulations regarding 'fleeting' use of expletives were ruled unconstitutionally vague by a three-judge panel of the U.S. 2nd Circuit Court of Appeals in New York on July 13, 2010.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The appeals court held that the rules violated the First Amendment due to vagueness; this is part of later jurisprudence that affects how isolated or inadvertent uses of expletives are regulated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcaster self-censorship practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcast networks generally censor themselves with regard to many of the seven dirty words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical practices include avoiding the words in scripted material and using bleep censoring (or other forms of redaction) when such words are used; enforcement and practices vary across outlets and times.

rubrics_metrics.name: FCC complaint and enforcement process (declaratory rulings and notices)
rubrics_metrics.description: After a complaint (e.g., the 1973 WBAI broadcast complaint), the FCC may ask a station for a response and issue a declaratory order upholding complaints; while initial orders may include no specific sanctions, a station can be put on notice that future complaints could lead to sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Pacifica sequence: complaint → FCC declaratory order (no immediate sanction) → appeals court reversal → Supreme Court review and decision; illustrates procedural steps and potential consequences for broadcasters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative attempts to codify a list of profane broadcasts (H.R. 3687)
rubrics_metrics.description: On December 8, 2003 Rep. Doug Ose introduced H.R. 3687, the 'Clean Airwaves Act', to designate a derivative list of Carlin's offensive words as profane in the U.S. Code; the bill listed words (e.g., shit, piss, fuck, cunt, asshole, cocksucker, motherfucker, the phrase 'ass hole').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bill's stated purpose was to amend 18 USC §1464 to provide punishment for certain profane broadcasts; the bill was not enacted, illustrating thatCongressional attempts to statutorily enumerate forbidden words have failed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited judicial scope regarding literary or religious uses
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court in Pacifica declined to consider whether the FCC's definition of 'indecency' would apply equally to broadcasts of other material containing the same words (e.g., works of Shakespeare or the Bible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This restraint suggests that identical words may be treated differently depending on context, artistic or religious value, and the specific circumstances of the broadcast.
